title: SECTION A — LACK, SCARCITY AND IDENTITY

questions.prompt: A therapist says, “I am going through a hard month financially, so I obviously have a poverty mindset.” What is the Zura distinction?
options: Anyone without spare money automatically has a poverty mindset.

Lack is a condition. Poverty mindset is not defined simply by whether someone presently has money. A person can be in financial difficulty and still be professional, generous, and growth-minded. The concern is when prolonged lack produces scarcity thinking and behaviour.
Poverty mindset only applies to clients, never staff.
If you are broke this month, excellence is postponed until you are rich.

questions.prompt: What does Zura mean by “poverty is not a product of lack”?
options: Lack never happens to professionals.
Poverty as a territory can form from a scarcity mindset after prolonged lack or down experiences — accepting lack as identity. Lack itself is not the identity.
Only people who have never lacked can serve wealthy clients.
Talking about money is always unprofessional.

questions.prompt: Which pattern is the actual mindset concern, not the fact of having less money this month?
options: Saving for rent while still delivering the full Zura standard.
Unnecessary rationing, cutting corners from fear, envy, badmouthing success, treating clients as “people with money,” or letting need weaken boundaries and standards.
Asking leadership a factual question about product use.
Feeling tired after a long shift.

questions.prompt: A client is talking about society and casually says, “All these poverty mindset,” not about you or the service. What should you do?
options: Go quiet and start proving you are not poor.
Join briefly and professionally: support that poverty mindset is not something to accommodate or build, then continue the service. Do not personalize a statement that was not directed at you.
Turn the massage into a debate about your salary.
Report the client immediately for insulting staff.

questions.prompt: You unnecessarily limited something the client should normally receive. They say, “Why are you managing this like this? All these poverty mindset.” What comes first?
options: “I don't have poverty mindset!” before fixing anything.

Listen → identify → acknowledge → correct. Apologize, fix the service, and make clear you do not support that mindset — it was an error, not your identity. You can accept the correction without absorbing the label.
Argue about how much money you have.
Ignore the service issue because the wording was rude.

title: SECTION B — LABELS, JUDGMENT AND SERVICE ERRORS

questions.prompt: The client says directly, “You have a poverty mindset.” What is the professional first move?
options: “Who are you calling poor?”
Ask what you did that gave that impression. Extract useful feedback about behaviour. Correct what is true. Do not automatically absorb the identity.
List your assets to win the argument.
Agree that you are poor so the client feels heard.

questions.prompt: The service issue is already corrected. The client continues: “That's how you people are. Poverty people.” How should you respond?
options: Shout about how much money you have, or insult the client.

Stay calm, refuse the personal label firmly: you are not poor, not in poverty territory, and do not operate under that mindset. Take responsibility for any error. Escalate if disrespect continues. Self-respect is not aggression.
Accept the humiliation so you remain “professional.”
Walk out of the session without communication.

questions.prompt: Why separate THE BEHAVIOUR from THE IDENTITY when a client uses “poverty mindset”?
options: So you never have to change anything you did.
There may be useful information inside an uncomfortable sentence. Correct the action. Do not let a label become who you are.
Because clients are never allowed to comment on service.
Because identity always matches the worst thing someone said.

questions.prompt: A client jokes, “Don't be doing poverty mindset. Pour plenty,” when you are using the correct product quantity. What is the trap?
options: Waste product so you do not look poor.
Do not confuse abundance with waste. Keep the legitimate standard. If needed: “I'll make sure you have what is appropriate for the service.” Responsible use is not scarcity identity.
Refuse all oil for the rest of the session.
Ask the client to pour it themselves.

questions.prompt: You were wrong on the service. You also refuse the identity “poverty-minded.” Can both be true?
options: No. If you apologize you must accept the whole label.
Yes. Admit the action was wrong without accepting a negative identity. The goal is to correct the client experience, not to win a status argument.
Yes, but only if management is in the room.
No. Never apologize if a client used a harsh word.

title: SECTION C — JEALOUSY, GOSSIP AND OTHER PEOPLE'S SUCCESS

questions.prompt: A client arrives in designer clothes and an expensive car. You catch yourself thinking they are “showing off.” What sequence matches the standard?
options: Joke about dirty money after they leave.
Notice → identify → stop comparison → return to your responsibility. Their possessions did not take your value. Serve the Zura standard.
Give extra-illegal favours so they like you.
Reduce pressure to “humble” them.

questions.prompt: After a wealthy client leaves, staff start mocking the vehicle, accent, and spending. What should you do?
options: Join because it is entertaining.
Redirect: if there is something relevant to service or operations, report it. Otherwise do not discuss the client's personal life. Clients are not staff entertainment.
Post it in a staff group with photos.
Only mock if the client was rude.

questions.prompt: Thr. B gets more tips and compliments. Thr. A starts saying, “Management just likes her” and “She's not even that good.” What is happening?
options: Healthy professional analysis.
An attempt to reduce someone else's value instead of improving. Use comparison as information: What can I learn? Raise genuine unfairness with facts. Otherwise grow.
Required competition under Driver–Passenger.
Proof that tips are always unfair.

questions.prompt: A client praises your co-therapist more and tips them more. You feel hurt. What question should you ask?
options: “How do I make the client regret that?”
“Is there anything professionally useful I can learn?” If yes, learn. If no, release it. Another person's appreciation does not diminish you.
“How do I report the colleague for stealing my tip?”
“Should I slow down my work next time so they look worse?”

questions.prompt: Whenever success is mentioned, a therapist immediately finds a fault: “They probably know somebody.” What should they ask themselves?
options: Nothing. Reducing people is harmless.
“Can I acknowledge another person's success without explaining it away?” If not, there may be insecurity. You do not need someone's light to dim before yours can shine.
“How do I get the client to confirm the gossip?”
“Should I only do this about staff, not clients?”

title: SECTION D — NEED, INFERIORITY AND BOUNDARIES

questions.prompt: Financial pressure makes you extra warm to clients you think will tip and flat with those you think will not. What failed?
options: Nothing. Need always decides service quality.
Personal need was allowed to control how you treat people. Separate need from professional responsibility. Tips are optional. The Zura standard is not.
You should only serve wealthy clients.
You should refuse all tips so you stay pure.

questions.prompt: A wealthy client makes you nervous. You start ignoring boundaries you would keep with anyone else, thinking they can “change your life.” What is the correction?
options: Wealth creates human superiority, so boundaries drop.
Respect success without making yourself smaller. They are a client. You are a professional. Same dignity, same boundaries, same Zura standard.
Ask them for a job during the massage.
Tolerate harassment so they book again.

questions.prompt: Scarcity can produce jealousy. What else can it produce toward a wealthy client?
options: Nothing else.
Inferiority and excessive admiration: trying too hard, speaking differently, seeking personal favour. Both jealousy and worship are distortions. Stay grounded.
Automatic friendship after one session.
The right to discuss their bank account with colleagues.

questions.prompt: A therapist treats a modest-spending client as less important than a high spender. Which mindset line is being broken?
options: Only Manager may grade clients by spend.
I can serve people with less without treating them as less important. I can serve wealthy people without feeling inferior. Spend does not set human value in the room.
Modest clients should get a shorter massage automatically.
High spenders must be addressed as Manager.

questions.prompt: A colleague says excellence is “for other people” because they are used to poor conditions. What is the danger?
options: None. Low standards feel honest.
Accepting low standards because poor conditions became familiar. Lack must not become identity or an excuse to stop being professional and better.
They should only improve after they get rich.
They should hide from assessments.

title: SECTION E — NOTICE, CORRECT AND SERVE

questions.prompt: You notice jealousy rising mid-session. What is the expected inner move?
options: Hide it and let it leak as cold service.
Identify it quickly and correct it. Drop associated midsts as soon as you notice them. Return to the client in front of you.
Tell the client you are jealous so you are honest.
Ask the co-therapist to gossip after.

questions.prompt: Is professional reporting of a real client concern the same as badmouthing their lifestyle?
options: Yes. Any talk about a client is gossip.
No. Ask: is this necessary for service or operations? If yes, report it. If no, leave it. Reporting is not entertainment.
Yes, if you whisper.
No, but mocking spending is allowed if you also file a report.

questions.prompt: A random “poverty mindset” comment was not about you, but you still felt stabbed. What mindset would have protected the session?
options: Every client sentence is about me.
Everything a client says is not about me. I do not need to prove my financial status. I can join a healthy conversation without becoming defensive.
I must never speak at all.
I should end the massage early.

questions.prompt: Which sequence matches the close of this issue?
options: COMPARE → BADMOUTH → HOARD → SHRINK
NOTICE → QUESTION → CORRECT → LEARN → IMPROVE → SERVE PROFESSIONALLY
ARGUE WEALTH → IGNORE SERVICE → ESCALATE EVERY JOKE
ACCEPT THE LABEL → LOWER THE STANDARD

questions.prompt: Someone else's success, wealth, or opportunity — what is it not evidence of?
options: That you must copy their lifestyle tonight.
Your failure, your inferiority, or the removal of your opportunity. Do not let temporary lack produce envy, badmouthing, insecurity, poor service, or reduced standards.
That they are always morally better.
That you should stop learning.
